title: Air India Ends Mainline International Flights From Chennai, Hands Singapore Route to Express
excerpt: Chennai–Singapore goes twice-daily on Air India Express 737 MAX 8s from October 25, while mainline adds a daily Chennai–Muscat service — part of a group-wide winter reshuffle that also drops Copenhagen.
body:
• Air India's Northern Winter 2026/27 schedule, effective October 25, ends the airline's mainline international operation from Chennai: the Chennai–Singapore service transfers to Air India Express, which will fly it twice daily with Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft.
  • The shift is part of a group-wide reallocation, not a withdrawal — Air India Express unveiled its largest winter network ever (585 daily flights, 105+ aircraft, 40+ new routes), while mainline Air India adds a daily non-stop A319 service between Chennai and Muscat.
  • Other winter changes: Air India drops Delhi–Copenhagen entirely after October 23, cancels Amritsar–London Gatwick, and trims Ahmedabad–London Gatwick from 4 to 3 weekly.
  • What it means for travellers: Chennai–Singapore keeps 14 weekly flights but moves to a low-cost cabin; book on Air India Express (IX628/IX630) from October 25, and expect mainline-to-Express aircraft and service differences on the route.

Air India's winter schedule brings a symbolic changing of the guard at Chennai airport. From October 25, the airline's mainline international operation from the Tamil Nadu capital comes to an end, as the Chennai–Singapore service transfers to its low-cost sister carrier Air India Express — a move that has sparked grumbling in Chennai even as the group insists the city is gaining, not losing, connectivity.

What changes

Under the Northern Winter 2026/27 schedule, Air India Express takes over Chennai–Singapore with twice-daily Boeing 737 MAX 8 flights. The Deccan Chronicle, which first flagged the change, notes Chennai also missed out on the resumption of Dubai, Sri Lanka, Sharjah and Kuala Lumpur services — routes stopped about three months earlier — IX628 and IX630 departing Chennai at 02:05 and 13:10, with returns IX627 and IX629. The schedule works out to 14 weekly frequencies, matching the route's current scale but in a single-aisle, low-cost configuration. Air India Express last served the route until July 2025.

The transfer marks the end of Air India mainline international flying from Chennai. But the picture is more complex than a retreat: the winter schedule also introduces a daily, non-stop A319 service between Chennai and Muscat on mainline Air India, and Air India Express's overall winter network is its largest ever — around 585 daily flights (435 domestic, up to 150 international) across 220 routes, with weekly flights jumping from about 3,150 in summer to nearly 4,100.

"The scale of the winter schedule reflects the airline's confidence in India's growth and the importance of air connectivity to trade, tourism and economic development," said Nipun Aggarwal, chairman of Air India Express, announcing the expansion.

Why it's happening

The Tata-group carriers are steadily redrawing the map between the two brands: full-service Air India concentrates wide-body, long-haul flying from Delhi and Mumbai, while Air India Express absorbs short- and medium-haul international routes. Similar logic drove the May rationalisation of selected international services, which the airline attributed to airspace restrictions and high jet-fuel prices.

Chennai is not alone in feeling the reshuffle. The winter update drops Delhi–Copenhagen entirely after October 23 — ending nonstop India–Denmark connectivity despite the route having been listed in Air India's March winter-network announcement — cancels the three-weekly Amritsar–London Gatwick service from October 26, and reduces Ahmedabad–London Gatwick from four to three weekly flights. On the plus side, Boeing 777s will now cover all seven westbound destinations plus Tokyo, and Mumbai–Riyadh and Delhi–Riyadh frequencies rise to 11 per week combined.

"The scale of the winter schedule reflects the airline's confidence in India's growth and the importance of air connectivity to trade, tourism and economic development."

— Nipun Aggarwal, Chairman, Air India Express

Diaspora angle

Chennai–Singapore is one of the busiest corridors for the Tamil diaspora — students, workers and families shuttling between Tamil Nadu and Southeast Asia. The route survives with the same frequency, but the product changes: travellers booking after October 25 will fly a 737 MAX 8 in Air India Express's low-cost cabin rather than a mainline aircraft, with different baggage, meal and loyalty-earn rules. For price-sensitive flyers the added competition-season capacity is good news; for premium and business travellers, the full-service option from Chennai is gone. Check whether your ticket is issued on Air India (AI) or Air India Express (IX) stock before assuming lounge access or through-checked baggage on connections.

What's next

The winter schedule rolls out in phases from October 25, so travellers should verify aircraft and operator on specific dates rather than assuming the old pattern holds. And with Air India Express adding more than 40 new routes this winter — from Bangkok–Visakhapatnam to Dubai–Goa — the group is betting that frequency and low fares matter more to Chennai's travellers than the mainline brand on the tail.
image_caption: An Air India Express Boeing 737 takes off from a runway. The carrier takes over the Chennai–Singapore route from mainline Air India on October 25, operating it twice daily.
